questions.prompt: What do sharp, flat, and natural signs do to a note?
choices: A Sharp lowers a tone; flat raises it; natural doubles the pitch.
B Sharp raises by a semitone; flat lowers by a semitone; natural cancels an alteration (play as “white-key” natural).
C All three only change duration, not pitch.
D They only apply outside the bar they appear in.
questions.explain: Sharp = +semitone, flat = −semitone, natural cancels; accidentals generally hold for the bar.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a melodic interval and a harmonic interval?
choices: A Melodic = simultaneous tones; harmonic = one after the other.
B Melodic = tones one after another; harmonic = tones played simultaneously.
C Melodic intervals only exist in jazz; harmonic only in chant.
D There is no difference in his terminology.
questions.explain: Melodic intervals are sequential; harmonic intervals are simultaneous.

questions.prompt: What tone–semitone pattern does he give for the major scale?
choices: A S–T–T–S–T–T–T
B Tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone–tone–semitone
C Only semitones throughout
D Tone–semitone repeated four times with no final semitone

questions.prompt: Why are C major and A minor called relative keys in this lecture?
choices: A They use opposite accidentals and never share tones.
B They share the same key signature (both use only white keys in his example).
C Relative means they must be played an octave apart only.
D They are identical scales with the same tonic.
questions.explain: A minor is the relative minor of C major; they share the same key signature / white-key collection.

questions.prompt: Which intervals does he class as perfect consonances?
choices: A Only major and minor thirds.
B Unison, fourth, fifth, and octave.
C Only tritones and sevenths.
D Augmented seconds exclusively.
questions.explain: Unison, fourth, fifth, and octave are treated as perfect consonances (simple ratios).
